title: Macedonia (ancient kingdom)
description: Ancient Greek kingdom in the southern Balkans
wiki_lead:
Macedonia (  MASS-ih-DOH-nee-ə; Greek: Μακεδονία, Makedonía), also called Macedon ( MASS-ih-don), was an ancient kingdom on the periphery of Archaic and Classical Greece, which later became the dominant state of Hellenistic Greece. The kingdom was founded and initially ruled by the royal Argead dynasty, which was followed by the Antipatrid and Antigonid dynasties. Home to the ancient Macedonians, the earliest kingdom was centred on the northeastern part of the Greek peninsula, and bordered by Epirus to the southwest, Illyria to the northwest, Paeonia to the north, Thrace to the east and Thessaly to the south. 
Before the 4th century BC, Macedonia was a small kingdom centered in Aegae, outside of the area dominated by the city-states of Athens, Sparta, and Thebes, and briefly subordinate to the Achaemenid Empire. During the reign of king Philip II (359–336 BC), Macedonia with its capital in Pella, subdued mainland Greece, Paeonia, and the Thracian Odrysian kingdom through conquest and diplomacy. With a reformed army containing phalanxes wielding the sarissa pike, Philip II defeated the old powers of Athens and Thebes at the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BC. Philip II's son Alexander the Great, became king of Macedon and leader of the League of Corinth founded by his father, and accomplished the objective of commanding the whole of Greece when he destroyed Thebes when the city revolted. During Alexander's subsequent campaign of conquest, he overthrew the Achaemenid Empire and conquered territory that stretched as far as the Indus River. For a brief period, his Macedonian Empire was the most powerful in the world – the definitive Hellenistic state, inaugurating the transition to a new period of Ancient Greek civilization. Greek arts and literature flourished in the new conquered lands and advances in philosophy, engineering, and science spread across the empire and beyond. Of particular importance were the contributions of Aristotle, tutor to Alexander, whose writings became a keystone of Western philosophy.
After Alexander's death in 323 BC, the ensuing wars of the Diadochi, and the partitioning of Alexander's short-lived empire, Macedonia remained a Greek cultural and political centre in the Mediterranean region along with Ptolemaic Egypt, the Seleucid Empire, and the Attalid kingdom. Important cities included its capital Pella, Dion, Beroea, Pydna, and Amphipolis, while new cities were founded, such as Thessalonica by the usurper Cassander (named after his wife Thessalonike of Macedon). Macedonia's decline began with the Second Macedonian War and the rise of Rome as the leading Mediterranean power. At the end of the Third Macedonian War in 168 BC, the Macedonian monarchy was abolished and replaced by Roman client states. A short-lived revival of the monarchy during the Fourth Macedonian War in 150–148 BC ended with the establishment of the Roman province of Macedonia.
The Macedonian kings, who wielded absolute power and commanded state resources such as gold and silver, facilitated mining operations to mint currency, finance their armies and, by the reign of Philip II, a Macedonian navy. Unlike the other diadochi successor states, the imperial cult fostered by Alexander was never adopted in Macedonia, yet Macedonian rulers nevertheless assumed roles as high priests of the kingdom and leading patrons of domestic and international cults of the Hellenistic religion. The authority of Macedonian kings was theoretically limited by the institution of the army, while a few municipalities within the Macedonian commonwealth enjoyed a high degree of autonomy and even had democratic governments with popular assemblies.

Etymology

The name Macedonia (Greek: Μακεδονία, Makedonía) comes from the ethnonym Μακεδόνες (Makedónes), which itself is derived from the ancient Greek adjective μακεδνός (makednós), meaning 'tall, slim', also the name of a people related to the Dorians (Herodotus), and possibly descriptive of Ancient Macedonians. grok_lead: The Kingdom of Macedonia was an ancient state located in northern Greece, centered at Pella in the northeastern Aegean region. Ruled by the Argead dynasty from the mid-seventh century BC until the late fourth century BC, it long existed as a fragmented backwater amid internal strife and external threats from neighboring tribes. In the mid-fourth century BC, Philip II ascended the throne in 359 BC and transformed Macedonia into the preeminent military power of the Greek world through administrative centralization, economic exploitation of resources like timber and silver mines, and military innovations such as the sarissa-equipped phalanx and integrated cavalry tactics. These reforms enabled decisive victories over Illyrians, Thracians, and Greek coalitions, including the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BC, which imposed Macedonian hegemony over the southern poleis via the League of Corinth. Philip's son, Alexander III, inherited this strengthened realm in 336 BC and launched campaigns that dismantled the Achaemenid Empire, founding cities and extending Macedonian influence to Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Indus Valley by his death in 323 BC. The kingdom's defining legacy lies in its role as the launchpad for Hellenistic expansion, blending Greek culture with eastern traditions despite subsequent dynastic wars and eventual Roman subjugation in 168 BC.
